assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision picture and its quantum theory made strong-field light–matter interaction intelligible and enabled high-harmonic generation to become a major route to ultrafast science. This is a fundamental conceptual advance with broad experimental reach.
assessment.attribution: Corkum supplied the influential classical recollision model; Lewenstein and Schafer helped establish its quantum and computational foundations. The field has many contributors, so a three-person attribution necessarily emphasizes the core model and theory.
assessment.maturity: The picture has been tested and extended across decades of strong-field experiments, and high-harmonic methods are now established in multiple laboratories.
uncertainties: The boundary between this theoretical advance and the experimental discovery and development of high-harmonic generation is difficult to draw.
A three-person award could omit experimental pioneers whose work was essential to the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry brought coherent matter waves into precision measurement, creating a powerful way to test quantum mechanics, gravity, and fundamental constants. Its capacity to reveal phase shifts with exceptional sensitivity gives it lasting scientific importance.
assessment.attribution: Bordé established early atom interferometry, while Pritchard and Kasevich made influential experimental contributions to its development and precision applications. The advances came through several complementary experiments.
assessment.maturity: The method has been reproduced and refined in many laboratories, with a long record of increasingly precise measurements.
uncertainties: The field developed through multiple interferometer designs, making any short list of inventors incomplete.
Some leading applications are still improving in precision, so the eventual scientific reach remains open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattices with ultracold atoms made controlled studies of strongly interacting quantum matter possible. The observation of a Mott-insulating transition and the broader quantum-simulation program opened a new experimental way to investigate many-body physics.
assessment.attribution: Greiner led the landmark Mott-transition experiment; Bloch developed the experimental platform and its applications; Zoller provided essential theoretical proposals for quantum simulation. Their complementary roles are well established.
assessment.maturity: The platform has been replicated and extended across many systems and laboratories, and it continues to yield robust results.
uncertainties: The nomination combines a specific experimental discovery with a broad program that includes many subsequent contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks transformed precision timekeeping by combining narrow optical transitions with control of atomic motion and systematic shifts. They enable stringent tests of fundamental physics as well as precision comparisons across space and time.
assessment.attribution: Katori and Ye independently developed leading realizations of the optical lattice clock, with distinct but complementary approaches. The central conceptual and experimental contributions are clearly associated with them.
assessment.maturity: Clock performance has been validated and improved by many groups over decades, establishing the technique as a mature precision measurement tool.
uncertainties: The Nobel case depends on weighing a major measurement advance against its broad metrological character.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov–Bohm effect and Berry phase show that quantum phases can have observable consequences beyond local forces, with influence across atomic, condensed-matter, and other areas of physics. This is a deep conceptual contribution to quantum mechanics.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and collaborators identified the physical significance of potentials in the Aharonov–Bohm effect; Berry formulated the general geometric phase for adiabatic evolution. These are distinct advances grouped under a common theme.
assessment.maturity: Both ideas have extensive experimental confirmation and have become standard tools in theoretical and experimental physics.
uncertainties: The ballot groups two related but historically distinct discoveries, and credit for the Aharonov–Bohm effect includes Aharonov's collaborators.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light overcomes measurement noise limits and has become a practical quantum resource for precision interferometry. It links quantum optics to demanding tests of nature, including gravitational-wave detection.
assessment.attribution: Caves established key theory for quantum-enhanced measurement; Kimble helped develop and demonstrate squeezed-light methods; Schnabel advanced high-performance squeezed-light sources and their use in precision interferometry. Other experimental contributors also deserve recognition.
assessment.maturity: The principle is experimentally established and has moved into operating precision instruments, while improvements continue.
uncertainties: The work spans theory, laboratory demonstrations, and large-scale detector implementation, complicating a compact attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping cold antimatter permits precision comparisons of matter and antimatter and stringent tests of fundamental symmetries. The achievement is technically formidable and directly addresses basic questions about nature.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse, Hangst, and Ulmer represent major experimental strands in trapping and precision measurement of antimatter. The work is necessarily collaborative, and credit extends to large teams.
assessment.maturity: Antihydrogen production, trapping, and spectroscopy have progressed through repeated experiments, though precision tests remain under active development.
uncertainties: The most decisive symmetry comparisons are still limited by experimental precision.
The scale of the collaborations makes individual attribution uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity QED interfaces made it possible to control and connect matter and photons, laying important foundations for quantum networks and tests of light–matter interaction at the single-quantum level.
assessment.attribution: Rempe and Kimble led influential experimental demonstrations of cavity-mediated atom–photon control; Cirac contributed foundational proposals for quantum networking. The area has many closely related experimental and theoretical contributions.
assessment.maturity: The basic interface physics is established and replicated, while scaling to large, reliable networks remains an ongoing effort.
uncertainties: The nominated discovery is broad and overlaps with several neighboring quantum-optics advances.
The full network vision is not yet mature at large scale.
